books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Fort Sumter crisis as told in 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 15, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 7, Topic 5.7. Dates, hours, and casualty figures verified against the National Park Service (nps.gov/apco/april-1861.htm) and the Battle of Fort Sumter record. The facts are as stated in the books; the wording is original.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase: Fort Sumter stood on an island in Charleston Harbor, one of the last federal forts still held in the seceded South. In April 1861 President Lincoln told South Carolina he would send food, but not men or arms, to the hungry garrison. Before the supply ships arrived, Confederate guns opened fire at 4:30 in the morning on April 12. After about thirty-four hours of bombardment, Major Robert Anderson surrendered the fort on April 13. No soldier was killed by the shelling. Two days later, on April 15, Lincoln called for 75,000 militiamen to put down the rebellion, and four more slave states — Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina — left the Union.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Lincoln's decision to send food, but not men or arms, is best understood as an attempt to

options.text: surrender the fort to the Confederacy without a fight.
options.misconception: Sending food kept the fort held; surrender would have meant giving it up.

options.text: trick the Confederacy into attacking Britain instead.
options.misconception: The passage says nothing about Britain; the supplies were for the fort's own garrison.

options.text: arm the garrison for a long siege at Charleston.
options.misconception: Food, not men or arms, is the point: Lincoln sent provisions, not reinforcements.

options.text: make the Confederacy fire first or let the fort stand.

rationales.A: Sending food kept the fort held; surrender would have meant giving it up.
rationales.B: The passage says nothing about Britain; the supplies were for the fort's own garrison.
rationales.C: Food, not men or arms, is the point: Lincoln sent provisions, not reinforcements.
rationales.D: By sending only food and announcing it in advance, Lincoln left the Confederacy the choice: fire on a supply mission or watch the fort hold out. Background: Lincoln needed the South to fire first so the North would unite behind the war.
rationales.general:
1. Food keeps the fort alive without threatening anyone.
2. Announcing it in advance removes any claim of surprise.
3. Background: Lincoln's cabinet was divided, and most of his advisers wanted to give the fort up.
4. The resupply was a move that made the other side move first.
Remember: a limited move can force an unlimited choice — ask what the other side must do next.
